title: Determine the Area of a Composite Figure
goal: I can split a figure into rectangles, find the area of each part, and add the parts.
catchAll: Split the figure into rectangles with no overlap. Find each area, then add them.

teacher.def: number of unit squares needed to cover the INSIDE of a shape or region
to find the area of a rectangle, you multiply the length and the width

glossary.composite figure: a figure made of two or more rectangles (or other shapes)
glossary.decompose: break a figure into smaller parts
glossary.partial area: the area of one part of the figure

screens.title: A composite figure
text: A composite figure is made of two or more rectangles joined together.
This L shape is not a rectangle, but it is made of two rectangles.
screens.caption: An L-shaped composite figure

screens.title: Decompose it
text: Decompose means break it into parts. Draw a line to make two rectangles that do not overlap.
Top part: 6 by 2. Bottom part: 2 by 3.
screens.caption: Two parts that do not overlap

screens.title: Explain My Thinking: why split the figure?

item.prompt: Why can a composite figure be divided into smaller rectangles? Write your answer in a sentence.
hints: What shapes are easy to find the area of? How can the figure be made from them?
item.example: A composite figure can be divided into smaller rectangles because its parts fit together, and we know how to find the area of each rectangle.
show: Write one sentence that answers the question.
Here is one way to say it: A composite figure can be divided into smaller rectangles because its parts fit together, and we know how to find the area of each rectangle.

screens.title: Area of each part, then add
text: Multiply to find each part's area: 6 × 2 = 12 and 2 × 3 = 6.
screens.caption: 12 + 6 = 18 square units

item.prompt: Finish it: the two parts are 12 and 6 square units.
hints: Add the two part areas.

screens.title: More than one way
text: You can split a figure in different ways. The total area stays the same.
Here the L is split the other way: 4 × 2 = 8 and 2 × 5 = 10. 8 + 10 = 18 again.
screens.caption: Another way: 8 + 10 = 18

screens.title: No overlaps
text: Each square of the figure must be in exactly one part.
If two parts overlap, the squares where they meet are counted twice.

screens.title: Explain My Thinking: why can we add the parts?

item.prompt: Why can we add the areas of two rectangles that do not overlap to find the area of the whole figure? Write your answer in a sentence.
hints: Think about what would go wrong if the rectangles overlapped, or left a gap.
item.example: We can add the areas because the rectangles cover the whole figure with no gaps and no overlap, so every square is counted once.
show: Write one sentence that answers the question.
Here is one way to say it: We can add the areas because the rectangles cover the whole figure with no gaps and no overlap, so every square is counted once.

screens.title: A missing part
text: If you know the whole area and one part, subtract to find the other part.
This figure covers 20 square units. The top part covers 12. The other part covers 20 - 12 = 8 square units.

screens.title: A missing side
text: Sometimes a side has no number. Use the sides you know.
The bottom is 8 units. The top part covers 5 of them. So the side marked ? is 8 - 5 = 3 units.
screens.caption: The ? side: 8 - 5 = 3

item.prompt: A figure is split into a 5 by 2 part and a 2 by 3 part that do not overlap. What is its area?

options.why: That is only the 5 by 2 part.
That adds the sides 5 + 2 + 2 + 3. Multiply each part, then add.

hints: Multiply each part: 5 × 2 and 2 × 3. Then add.

watch.takeaway: Decompose the composite figure into rectangles that do not overlap, find each area, and add the areas.

steps.say: Problem: what is the area of the L-shaped figure?
Step 1: Draw a line to split it into two rectangles that do not overlap.
Step 2: Top part: 6 long and 2 wide.
Step 3: Bottom part: 2 long and 3 wide.
Step 5: The area is 18 square units.

why.prompt: Why do we add the two areas?

options.text: Together the parts cover the whole figure.

options.why: It is not about easy. The two parts make the whole figure.
Multiplying 12 × 6 would be far too big. The parts are added.

why.yes: Yes! The parts together are the whole figure.

steps.say: Problem: a playground has this shape. What is its area?

examples.title: Example C: the same figure, split another way

steps.say: Problem: split the same playground with a line going across.

items.prompt: Mia split this U into three rectangles. She wrote: 2 × 5 = 10, 2 × 5 = 10, 10 + 10 = 20 square inches. Find Mia's mistake.

options.why: Her two tall rectangles do not overlap. Each square is counted once, but one part of the U is missing.

options.text: She found a partial area wrong.
options.why: 2 × 5 = 10 is right for each tall rectangle. The mistake is a part that has no area in her work.
10 + 10 = 20 is a true sum. The problem is that a part is missing from it.

options.text: Yes. Both splits cover the whole L with no overlap, so both find 18 square feet.
No. Only Student A is right, because a figure must be split with a line going across.

options.text: No. Only Student B is right, because the pieces must be tall.
options.why: The pieces do not have to be tall. They only have to be rectangles that cover the figure with no gaps and no overlap. Student A's pieces do.

options.text: No. Different splits must give different answers.
options.why: It is the same figure, so it has the same area. 12 + 6 = 18 and 10 + 8 = 18.

hints: Look at each picture. Do the two rectangles cover the whole L, with no gaps and no overlap?

sections.heading: What your child is learning
sections.text: Your child finds the area of a composite figure (a shape made of rectangles): split it into rectangles that do not overlap, multiply to find each part's area, then add.

sections.heading: Try it with real things
list: Draw an L shape on graph paper. Split it two different ways and check the totals match.
Look for L-shaped rooms, patios or rugs and estimate their parts.

sections.heading: Questions to ask
list: Where can you draw a line to make two rectangles?
What are the length and width of each part?
Did you add every part once?

sections.heading: Common mistakes
list: Finding one part and forgetting to add the other.
Using a side length that belongs to the whole figure for a part.
Splitting so that two parts overlap.
